business_patterns.top_pattern: Authorization coding and facility mapping shifts are distorting the read
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial inpatient authorization classification and facility mapping
business_patterns.pattern_details: A large share of the apparent cost movement is tied to authorization code redistribution rather than a clean underlying utilization trend. In both Colorado and Maine, dollars moved sharply out of the negative or unknown authorization bucket while both PA-required and non-PA segments increased, and Colorado also shows a meaningful rise in claims tied to an unmapped facility bucket. Validate coding and mapping first so downstream policy, UM, and network actions are aimed at real cost drivers.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: If the authorization and mapping fields are unstable, the business may overreact to the wrong segment, provider, or policy lever.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Audit PA-required code assignment and facility mapping in Colorado and Maine, reconcile the drop in the negative authorization bucket, and re-baseline any UM or reimbursement actions only after the data is corrected.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Large dollars shifted out of negative or unmapped buckets, indicating classification movement that can misstate the true source of cost change.
evidence_summary: Colorado authorization distribution shifted by about $57.1M in gross movement: PA Y +$19.3M, PA N +$9.9M, and the negative bucket -$28.0M.
Maine showed the same pattern: PA Y +$10.6M, PA N +$3.9M, and the negative bucket -$8.3M.
Colorado also added +$1.5M in a Not Mapped facility bucket, including 10 admissions at about $145.8K per admit.
The same authorization redistribution appears again in provider and DRG views, including chemotherapy, cesarean, craniotomy, and ungroupable claims.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Commercial HMO acute hospital admissions surged in Colorado and Maine
business_patterns.pattern_details: Commercial HMO inpatient spend rose sharply in acute hospitals, led by Colorado and Maine and reinforced by growth at Emory Decatur in Georgia. The biggest segments show very large admission growth, and several also show higher paid per admit, although some non-PA segments grew mainly from volume. This is a broad acute hospital utilization problem first, with unit-cost pressure layering on top in the largest segments.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: This is the largest actionable cost pattern and it points directly to acute inpatient management, local market strategy, and hospital contract exposure.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Prioritize Colorado and Maine for joint UM and network review, focusing on admission appropriateness, level of care, and hospital reimbursement in HMO acute settings.
evidence_summary: Colorado HMO acute hospital PA Y spend rose +$17.6M, with 517 more admissions and paid per admit up about $14.5K.
Maine HMO acute hospital PA Y spend rose +$10.1M, with 161 more admissions and paid per admit up about $1.1K.
Colorado HMO acute hospital PA N rose +$8.1M on 397 more admissions even though paid per admit fell about $15.8K, confirming a strong volume effect.
Emory Decatur added about +$1.9M across HMO PA Y and PA N segments, driven by roughly 110 additional admissions.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Provider concentration is raising acute hospital spend at Yale and Henrico
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial PPO/POS/EPO / Acute Hospital inpatient / selected providers
business_patterns.pattern_details: Spend is concentrating in a small set of acute hospital provider and product combinations, especially Yale New Haven and Henrico Doctors. Yale shows a mix of higher admissions and modestly higher paid per admit, while Henrico shows clearer reimbursement pressure with relatively flat admissions but much higher paid per admit in key PPO and POS segments. Smaller PPO and EPO acute segments add to the same provider-driven economics story.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Provider-specific economics can often be improved faster through contracting, steerage, and product rules than through broad population-wide interventions.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Run provider-specific reimbursement and steerage reviews for Yale New Haven and Henrico, comparing paid per admit and admission mix against local peers by product.
evidence_summary: Yale New Haven PPO non-PA spend rose +$2.4M, with 36 more admissions and paid per admit up about $4.4K.
Yale New Haven PPO PA Y added +$1.6M with 41 more admissions, showing continued provider concentration even without unit-cost growth.
Henrico POS non-PA added +$0.9M while admissions were flat to down and paid per admit increased about $13.4K.
Henrico PPO and POS segments added another +$0.3M, with paid per admit increases of about $10.9K to $19.8K.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Site-of-care is shifting into residential, children’s, and critical access facilities
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial inpatient / Residential Treatment, Children's, and Critical Access facilities
business_patterns.pattern_details: Inpatient spend is moving beyond standard acute hospitals into residential treatment, children's hospitals, and critical access facilities, primarily in Maine and Colorado. Residential treatment is the largest change, while children's and critical access segments are smaller but costly and often emerging from low baseline. This is a site-of-care and provider mix shift that needs different rules than routine acute inpatient management.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A shift into alternate facility types changes both the clinical management approach and the contract exposure.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Review admission criteria, redirect opportunities, and contracted rates by alternate facility type, starting with Maine residential treatment and Colorado children's and critical access facilities.
evidence_summary: Maine PPO residential treatment added +$3.5M, with 120 more admissions and paid per admit up about $15.8K.
Colorado HMO residential treatment added +$0.7M from 47 admissions that were not present in baseline.
Colorado children's facility spend rose +$1.6M across PA Y and PA N segments, with very high paid per admit.
Colorado critical access added +$0.6M on 23 new admissions.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Rare catastrophic Med/Surg cases are creating one-off cost shocks
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial inpatient Med/Surg / catastrophic transplant, ECMO, trach, and other complex outlier cases
key_driver_codes: Heart Transplant or Implant of Heart Assist System with MCC
ECMO or Tracheostomy with Mechanical Ventilation >96 Hours
Major Small and Large Bowel Procedures with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: A small number of catastrophic Med/Surg admissions drove a disproportionate share of cost change, including heart transplant or assist-device cases, ECMO and tracheostomy cases, major bowel surgery, and other one-off complex admissions. These are not broad utilization trends; they are case-level shocks with very high paid per admit. They should be handled as large-case management and validation work, not as routine trend management.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A handful of ultra-high-cost admissions can materially distort trend reporting and require separate clinical, financial, and stop-loss review.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Send these cases for case-level clinical validation and large-loss financial review, including contract terms, eligibility, and stop-loss or reinsurance treatment.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Most of the spend comes from new or very low-baseline cases with one to three admissions, so case-level validation is required before broader business conclusions are drawn.
evidence_summary: One Maine ECMO or trach case added about +$1.0M on a single admission.
Heart transplant or assist-device cases in Maine and at Yale added about +$1.6M across 2 admissions.
Tracheostomy outlier cases across Emory and Henrico added about +$0.5M across 3 admissions.
Other low-baseline complex Med/Surg outliers, including bowel surgery and neurologic cases, added roughly +$5.1M.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Inpatient chemotherapy is leading a high-intensity Med/Surg episode cluster
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial inpatient oncology and other high-intensity Med/Surg episodes
key_driver_codes: Chemotherapy without Acute Leukemia as Secondary Diagnosis with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: Within a focused cluster of high-intensity Med/Surg episodes, inpatient chemotherapy is the dominant driver. Chemotherapy admissions rose meaningfully and paid per admit increased sharply, while a smaller children's segment shows very high per-admit cost. There are also smaller non-oncology diagnoses in the same cluster, so oncology actions should be based on the chemotherapy subset rather than the entire cluster.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Inpatient oncology has different UM, site-of-care, and contracting levers than general Med/Surg admissions.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Isolate the chemotherapy subset and review inpatient-to-outpatient redirection opportunities, oncology case rates, and high-cost children's oncology arrangements.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The largest clinical group also contains smaller non-oncology Med/Surg episodes, so the oncology subset should be separated before changing policy or network strategy.
evidence_summary: Chemotherapy encounters added +$1.5M, with 11 more admissions and paid per admit up about $56.3K.
A children's EPO chemotherapy segment added +$0.6M from 2 admissions at about $296.3K per admit.
Smaller non-oncology diagnoses in the same high-intensity cluster contributed another roughly +$1.1M and should be separated from oncology-specific action.

business_patterns.top_pattern: C-section costs are rising with more high-acuity maternity cases
key_driver_codes: Cesarean Section without Sterilization without CC/MCC
MAT CARE LW TRANS SCAR PREV C/S DEL
business_patterns.pattern_details: C-section spend increased because both delivery volume and case acuity moved up. The largest drivers were hypertension and pre-eclampsia, post-term pregnancy, prior C-section history, and fetal heart rate complications, with a smaller set of very high-cost maternity outliers layered on top. This is a maternity-specific pattern and should be managed through obstetric clinical pathways and hospital reimbursement rather than general inpatient tactics.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Maternity cost growth often responds best to targeted obstetric care pathways, admission management, and hospital case-rate design.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Review CA maternity pathways and reimbursement for higher-acuity C-section cases, including prior C-section management and escalation triggers for complex pregnancies.
evidence_summary: Higher-acuity maternal conditions added about +$1.4M, led by pre-existing hypertension or pre-eclampsia at +$0.4M and post-term pregnancy at +$0.4M.
Prior C-section history added +$0.3M with 21 more admissions and little unit-cost change, showing more volume than price.
Rare maternity outliers, including monoamniotic twin pregnancy and vasa previa, added about +$0.7M across 2 admissions.
Abnormal fetal heart rate complications added +$0.3M with 18 more admissions.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Maine inpatient behavioral health is rising around alcohol-related admissions
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial inpatient behavioral health / alcohol-related admissions
key_driver_codes: Alcohol, Drug Abuse or Dependence without Rehabilitation Therapy without MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: Maine is showing a concentrated inpatient behavioral health increase tied to alcohol-related admissions. Both alcohol withdrawal and uncomplicated alcohol dependence segments grew, with more admissions and materially higher paid per admit. This looks like a focused BH access and utilization issue rather than general medical trend inflation.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Behavioral health growth requires different network, level-of-care, and step-down actions than acute medical admissions.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Review BH admission criteria, step-down and residential alternatives, and provider arrangements for alcohol-related inpatient stays in Maine.
evidence_summary: Alcohol withdrawal admissions in Maine added +$1.3M from 40 admissions starting from no baseline activity.
Uncomplicated alcohol dependence added +$0.9M with 34 more admissions and paid per admit up about $13.1K.
Together, the 2 alcohol-related BH segments contributed nearly 80 additional admissions over the period.

executive_summary.headline: The biggest business story is that acute inpatient cost growth is being amplified by authorization classification shifts, HMO acute admission surges, concentrated provider economics, and a handful of distinct clinical programs and outliers.
executive_summary.primary_business_message: Before changing authorization policy, validate the large PA code and mapping shifts because they materially affect how the increase is labeled. Once validated, the clearest business actions are to address HMO acute hospital growth in Colorado and Maine, provider-specific economics at Yale and Henrico, and site-of-care shifts into residential, children's, and critical access facilities, while handling oncology, maternity, behavioral health, and catastrophic cases with tailored clinical and financial pathways.
recommended_focus_order: Validate PA and facility mapping shifts first.
Attack HMO acute hospital growth in Colorado and Maine.
Address concentrated provider and site-of-care economics at Yale, Henrico, Maine residential treatment, and Colorado alternate facilities.

notes: All 24 analytical groups were assigned to a business pattern.
Authorization redistribution and unmapped facility activity were consolidated into one gating validation pattern.
Oncology, maternity, behavioral health, and rare catastrophic Med/Surg outliers were kept separate because their business actions differ.
Several clinical patterns include low-baseline cases; those should be handled with case-level review rather than broad trend assumptions.
